title: Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum

deep.reconstruction:
Sections VII–IX of E297 (Novi Commentarii 10, 1764/1766). Euler restates the variational problem in a purely analytic setting, as part of his re-derivation of Lagrange's δ-method (Lagrange is credited on the preceding page).

VII (the problem). The functional is J[y] = ∫_0^a Z dx. Z may depend on x, y and the derivatives p = y', q = y'', r = y''', etc. It may also contain embedded integral formulas, that is, non-local terms such as ∫_0^x W dx. The integral is normalised to vanish at x = 0 and evaluated at x = a, giving A = J[y]. The task is to find the relation between x and y (finite or a differential equation of any order) that makes A extremal. Finding that relation counts as solving the problem.

VIII (the functional as a Riemann sum). Suppose the relation y(x) is already known. Let x run from 0 to a in steps dx. Then A is the sum of the terms Z(x_i)·dx. The extremum property is stated as a comparison: for any other relation y*(x), the resulting A* is smaller (for a maximum) or larger (for a minimum) than A.

IX (first-variation principle). Now let the change in each value of y be infinitely small. By the nature of maxima and minima, A must then undergo no change: δA = 0. One computes the induced change in every term Z dx, sums it, and sets the total to zero. This yields the equation of the extremal, in modern terms the Euler–Lagrange equation. Euler stresses that this rests on the same principle as the ordinary calculus of maxima and minima, f'(x) = 0. He sets out to show it can be done by analysis alone, without the geometric constructions of his 1744 Methodus inveniendi.

The page is programmatic and definitional. No computation is carried out yet; the variation of the differentials is treated on later pages.
errors: No error of computation (there is none on the page). Conceptual gap: the extremum is defined globally ('ex alia relatione quacunque … certe minor'), but δA = 0 is only a necessary condition for a local (weak) extremum. Euler does not distinguish weak from strong or local from global extrema, and gives no sufficiency condition. That condition is Legendre 1786 and Jacobi 1836, with Weierstrass for strong extrema.
Boundary behaviour of the variations at x = 0 and x = a (fixed or free endpoints) is not specified here.

ideas.what: General functional ∫Z dx with Z depending on y and derivatives of any order, plus embedded integral formulas
ideas.where_published: E65 Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas (1744), chs. 2–3; also E296

ideas.what: The functional conceived as a sum of Z·dx over infinitesimal steps from x = 0 to x = a
ideas.modern_name: Discretisation / direct-method (Riemann-sum) view of a functional

ideas.what: Arbitrary infinitesimal variations applied to all values of y simultaneously; setting the first variation of A to zero
ideas.where_published: E296 Elementa calculi variationum and E297 (both Novi Comm. 10, 1766)

ideas.what: Explicit analogy between the variational extremum and the ordinary condition f' = 0
ideas.modern_name: Stationarity of a functional (Fermat's rule in function space)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard, well-documented programmatic passage in Euler's adoption of Lagrange's variational method. Its content (the Riemann-sum view of the functional and the first-variation principle) is fully covered in the histories of the calculus of variations (e.g. Goldstine, Fraser, Carathéodory's Opera omnia introduction).
transcription_corrections: 'Hic igitur operatione' should likely read 'Hac igitur operatione' (from the image and the grammar).
